content.text: Read the following passage from Frankenstein. This excerpt is narrated by the creature created by Victor Frankenstein. The creature describes some of his first experiences in the world following his creation and subsequent abandonment by Frankenstein.

textContent.text: One day, when I was oppressed by cold, I found a fire which had been left by some wandering beggars, and was overcome with delight at the warmth I experienced from it. In my joy I thrust my hand into the live embers, but quickly drew it out again with a cry of pain. How strange, I thought, that the same cause should produce such opposite effects! […]

It was about seven in the morning, and I longed to obtain food and shelter; at length I perceived a small hut, on a rising ground, which had doubtless been built for the convenience of some shepherd. This was a new sight to me, and I examined the structure with great curiosity. Finding the door open, I entered. An old man sat in it, near a fire, over which he was preparing his breakfast. He turned on hearing a noise, and perceiving me, shrieked loudly, and quitting the hut, ran across the fields with a speed of which his debilitated form hardly appeared capable. His appearance, different from any I had ever before seen, and his flight somewhat surprised me. But I was enchanted by the appearance of the hut; here the snow and rain could not penetrate; the ground was dry; and it presented to me then as exquisite and divine a retreat as Pandæmonium¹ appeared to the dæmons of hell after their sufferings in the lake of fire. I greedily devoured the remnants of the shepherd's breakfast, which consisted of bread, cheese, milk, and wine; the latter, however, I did not like. Then, overcome by fatigue, I lay down among some straw and fell asleep.

It was noon when I awoke, and allured by the warmth of the sun, which shone brightly on the white ground, I determined to recommence my travels; and, depositing the remains of the peasant's breakfast in a wallet I found, I proceeded across the fields for several hours, until at sunset I arrived at a village. How miraculous did this appear! The huts, the neater cottages, and stately houses engaged my admiration by turns. The vegetables in the gardens, the milk and cheese that I saw placed at the windows of some of the cottages, allured my appetite. One of the best of these I entered, but I had hardly placed my foot within the door before the children shrieked, and one of the women fainted. The whole village was roused; some fled, some attacked me, until, grievously bruised by stones and many other kinds of missile weapons, I escaped to the open country and fearfully took refuge in a low hovel, quite bare, and making a wretched appearance after the palaces I had beheld in the village. This hovel however, joined a cottage of a neat and pleasant appearance, but after my late dearly bought experience, I dared not enter it. My place of refuge was constructed of wood, but so low that I could with difficulty sit upright in it. No wood, however, was placed on the earth, which formed the floor, but it was dry; and although the wind entered it by innumerable chinks, I found it an agreeable asylum from the snow and rain.
Here, then, I retreated and lay down happy to have found a shelter, however miserable, from the inclemency of the season, and still more from the barbarity of man.
1. Pandæmonium is the capital of Hell in John Milton's epic poem Paradise Lost. In Milton's work, the fallen angels find refuge in Pandæmonium after being expelled from Heaven.
<citation>Adapted from Mary Wollstonecraft Shelley, Frankenstein; or, The Modern Prometheus</citation>

contents.text: The details in these two quotes suggest that the creature is naive and ignorant about the world:

text.text: In my joy I thrust my hand into the live embers, but quickly drew it out again with a cry of pain.

explanationText.text: The creature lacks common knowledge about the dangers of fire. Drawn to the warmth of the fire, he is completely unaware that the embers will burn him when he touches them.

text.text: This was a new sight to me, and I examined the structure with great curiosity. Finding the door open, I entered.

explanationText.text: The creature's reaction to finding the hut shows that he is unfamiliar with basic human structures. His instinct to simply enter upon finding the door open further illustrates his lack of understanding regarding norms of privacy and property.

contents.text: The creature had previously entered an impressive house in a village, and as a result, everyone in the village either ran away or grievously assaulted him for his intrusion. He now realizes that entering human houses can have unpleasant repercussions and decides not to enter the cottage despite his attraction to its "neat and pleasant appearance."
The creature's decision to forgo the pleasant cottage in favor of the lowly hovel demonstrates that he is learning from his previous mistakes and experiences.

content.text: Review the passage.

textContent.text: One day, when I was oppressed by cold, I found a fire which had been left by some wandering beggars, and was overcome with delight at the warmth I experienced from it. In my joy I thrust my hand into the live embers, but quickly drew it out again with a cry of pain. How strange, I thought, that the same cause should produce such opposite effects! […]

It was about seven in the morning, and I longed to obtain food and shelter; at length I perceived a small hut, on a rising ground, which had doubtless been built for the convenience of some shepherd. This was a new sight to me, and I examined the structure with great curiosity. Finding the door open, I entered. An old man sat in it, near a fire, over which he was preparing his breakfast. He turned on hearing a noise, and perceiving me, shrieked loudly, and quitting the hut, ran across the fields with a speed of which his debilitated form hardly appeared capable. His appearance, different from any I had ever before seen, and his flight somewhat surprised me. But I was enchanted by the appearance of the hut; here the snow and rain could not penetrate; the ground was dry; and it presented to me then as exquisite and divine a retreat as Pandæmonium¹ appeared to the dæmons of hell after their sufferings in the lake of fire. I greedily devoured the remnants of the shepherd's breakfast, which consisted of bread, cheese, milk, and wine; the latter, however, I did not like. Then, overcome by fatigue, I lay down among some straw and fell asleep.

It was noon when I awoke, and allured by the warmth of the sun, which shone brightly on the white ground, I determined to recommence my travels; and, depositing the remains of the peasant's breakfast in a wallet I found, I proceeded across the fields for several hours, until at sunset I arrived at a village. How miraculous did this appear! The huts, the neater cottages, and stately houses engaged my admiration by turns. The vegetables in the gardens, the milk and cheese that I saw placed at the windows of some of the cottages, allured my appetite. One of the best of these I entered, but I had hardly placed my foot within the door before the children shrieked, and one of the women fainted. The whole village was roused; some fled, some attacked me, until, grievously bruised by stones and many other kinds of missile weapons, I escaped to the open country and fearfully took refuge in a low hovel, quite bare, and making a wretched appearance after the palaces I had beheld in the village. This hovel however, joined a cottage of a neat and pleasant appearance, but after my late dearly bought experience, I dared not enter it. My place of refuge was constructed of wood, but so low that I could with difficulty sit upright in it. No wood, however, was placed on the earth, which formed the floor, but it was dry; and although the wind entered it by innumerable chinks, I found it an agreeable asylum from the snow and rain.
Here, then, I retreated and lay down happy to have found a shelter, however miserable, from the inclemency of the season, and still more from the barbarity of man.
1. Pandæmonium is the capital of Hell in John Milton's epic poem Paradise Lost. In Milton's work, the fallen angels find refuge in Pandæmonium after being expelled from Heaven.
<citation>Adapted from Mary Wollstonecraft Shelley, Frankenstein; or, The Modern Prometheus</citation>

contents.text: The details in the passage suggest this about the creature's appearance:

text.text: He has a large build and a hideous and inhuman face.

explanationText.text: The man in the hut and the people in the village react to their first sight of the creature by screaming, fleeing, or attacking him, which suggests that there is something monstrous and frightening about his appearance. The creature is unable to sit upright in the hovel, which suggests that he is large in build.

contents.text: The details in the passage do not suggest the following about the creature's appearance:

text.text: He covers himself with heavy clothing so no one can see what he looks like.

explanationText.text: The passage does not mention the creature using clothing to conceal his appearance. The reactions from humans suggest his appearance is fully visible and striking enough to cause fear and aggression, indicating that he does not hide what he looks like.

text.text: His body language suggests that he is ready to attack those who cross him.

explanationText.text: The passage does not mention any aggressive body language. The fact that the creature flees the village when attacked rather than fighting back suggests that he is not prepared to engage in violence at this time.

text.text: He always wears an angry and intimidating facial expression.

explanationText.text: The creature approaches the old man's hut and the houses in the village with interest and curiosity, not anger. He mentions that he is "overcome with delight" by the warmth of the fire and that the buildings in the village "engaged [his] admiration by turns." These details suggest that it is unlikely that the creature always wears an angry and intimidating facial expression.

content.text: How does the author portray the creature as innocent and inexperienced?

choices.text: by showing his tendency to overreact and lose his temper
by showing his preference for solitude over human contact
by showing his limited capacity for reason and perspective

contents.text: The details in the passage suggest that this is how the author portrays the creature as innocent and inexperienced:

text.text: by showing his wonder and delight in common and mundane things

explanationText.text: The reactions of the creature being "overcome with delight at the warmth" of the fire and his naive entry into strangers' homes all serve as a contrast to the reactions of the people who, upon seeing him, immediately shriek and attack him.

contents.text: These are not ways in which the author portrays the creature as innocent and inexperienced:

text.text: by showing his tendency to overreact and lose his temper

explanationText.text: When people attack the creature, he responds by fleeing rather than fighting back. This suggests that he does not lose his temper or react aggressively within this passage.

text.text: by showing his preference for solitude over human contact

explanationText.text: The creature's solitude is not a matter of preference but rather a consequence of societal rejection.

text.text: by showing his limited capacity for reason and perspective

explanationText.text: The creature shows the ability to reason when he reflects on and learns from his experiences. He demonstrates his capacity for perspective when he expresses gratitude for the shelter he finds, despite it being a ""miserable"" hovel.

But I was enchanted by the appearance of the hut; here the snow and rain could not penetrate; the ground was dry; and it presented to me then as exquisite and divine a retreat as Pandæmonium¹ appeared to the dæmons of hell after their sufferings in the lake of fire. textContent.text: It was noon when I awoke, and allured by the warmth of the sun, which shone brightly on the white ground, I determined to recommence my travels; and, depositing the remains of the peasant's breakfast in a wallet I found, I proceeded across the fields for several hours, until at sunset I arrived at a village. How miraculous did this appear! The huts, the neater cottages, and stately houses engaged my admiration by turns. The vegetables in the gardens, the milk and cheese that I saw placed at the windows of some of the cottages, allured my appetite. One of the best of these I entered, but I had hardly placed my foot within the door before the children shrieked, and one of the women fainted. The whole village was roused; some fled, some attacked me, until, grievously bruised by stones and many other kinds of missile weapons, I escaped to the open country and fearfully took refuge in a low hovel, quite bare, and making a wretched appearance after the palaces I had beheld in the village. This hovel however, joined a cottage of a neat and pleasant appearance, but after my late dearly bought experience, I dared not enter it. My place of refuge was constructed of wood, but so low that I could with difficulty sit upright in it. No wood, however, was placed on the earth, which formed the floor, but it was dry; and although the wind entered it by innumerable chinks, I found it an agreeable asylum from the snow and rain.
Here, then, I retreated and lay down happy to have found a shelter, however miserable, from the inclemency of the season, and still more from the barbarity of man.

contents.text: The details in the passage suggest that this is how the author portrays the creature as innocent and inexperienced:

text.text: by showing his wonder and delight in common and mundane things

explanationText.text: The reactions of the creature being "overcome with delight at the warmth" of the fire and his naive entry into strangers' homes all serve as a contrast to the reactions of the people who, upon seeing him, immediately shriek and attack him.

contents.text: These are not ways in which the author portrays the creature as innocent and inexperienced:

text.text: by showing his tendency to overreact and lose his temper

explanationText.text: When people attack the creature, he responds by fleeing rather than fighting back. This suggests that he does not lose his temper or react aggressively within this passage.

text.text: by showing his limited capacity for reason and perspective

explanationText.text: The creature shows the ability to reason when he reflects on and learns from his experiences. He demonstrates his capacity for perspective when he expresses gratitude for the shelter he finds, despite it being a ""miserable"" hovel.

text.text: by showing his preference for solitude over human contact

explanationText.text: The creature's solitude is not a matter of preference but rather a consequence of societal rejection.

contents.text: The creature had previously entered an impressive house in a village, and as a result, everyone in the village either ran away or grievously assaulted him for his intrusion. He now realizes that entering human houses can have unpleasant repercussions and decides not to enter the cottage despite his attraction to its "neat and pleasant appearance."
The creature's decision to forgo the pleasant cottage in favor of the lowly hovel demonstrates that he is learning from his previous mistakes and experiences.

content.text: Review the passage.

textContent.text: One day, when I was oppressed by cold, I found a fire which had been left by some wandering beggars, and was overcome with delight at the warmth I experienced from it. In my joy I thrust my hand into the live embers, but quickly drew it out again with a cry of pain. How strange, I thought, that the same cause should produce such opposite effects! […]

It was about seven in the morning, and I longed to obtain food and shelter; at length I perceived a small hut, on a rising ground, which had doubtless been built for the convenience of some shepherd. This was a new sight to me, and I examined the structure with great curiosity. Finding the door open, I entered. An old man sat in it, near a fire, over which he was preparing his breakfast. He turned on hearing a noise, and perceiving me, shrieked loudly, and quitting the hut, ran across the fields with a speed of which his debilitated form hardly appeared capable. His appearance, different from any I had ever before seen, and his flight somewhat surprised me. But I was enchanted by the appearance of the hut; here the snow and rain could not penetrate; the ground was dry; and it presented to me then as exquisite and divine a retreat as Pandæmonium¹ appeared to the dæmons of hell after their sufferings in the lake of fire. I greedily devoured the remnants of the shepherd's breakfast, which consisted of bread, cheese, milk, and wine; the latter, however, I did not like. Then, overcome by fatigue, I lay down among some straw and fell asleep.

It was noon when I awoke, and allured by the warmth of the sun, which shone brightly on the white ground, I determined to recommence my travels; and, depositing the remains of the peasant's breakfast in a wallet I found, I proceeded across the fields for several hours, until at sunset I arrived at a village. How miraculous did this appear! The huts, the neater cottages, and stately houses engaged my admiration by turns. The vegetables in the gardens, the milk and cheese that I saw placed at the windows of some of the cottages, allured my appetite. One of the best of these I entered, but I had hardly placed my foot within the door before the children shrieked, and one of the women fainted. The whole village was roused; some fled, some attacked me, until, grievously bruised by stones and many other kinds of missile weapons, I escaped to the open country and fearfully took refuge in a low hovel, quite bare, and making a wretched appearance after the palaces I had beheld in the village. This hovel however, joined a cottage of a neat and pleasant appearance, but after my late dearly bought experience, I dared not enter it. My place of refuge was constructed of wood, but so low that I could with difficulty sit upright in it. No wood, however, was placed on the earth, which formed the floor, but it was dry; and although the wind entered it by innumerable chinks, I found it an agreeable asylum from the snow and rain.
Here, then, I retreated and lay down happy to have found a shelter, however miserable, from the inclemency of the season, and still more from the barbarity of man.

explanationText.text: The passage focuses on the creature's desire for food and shelter and his curiosity about the world around him. He does not express loneliness or a desire to make friends in the passage.

explanationText.text: In the passage, the creature is not shy about approaching humans, and he doesn't flee from them until he is physically attacked.

contents.text: Which statement primarily appeals to pathos, or emotion, to support the position that people are too willing to go along with those in positions of authority?

choices.text: I, for one, refuse to be a trusting sheep led to slaughter or a mindless lemming guided off a cliff.

The experiments of Stanley Milgram have shown that we often defer to authority figures, such as experimenters in lab coats, even when we're dubious about or uncomfortable with what they instruct us to do.

contents.text: The purpose of many writing tasks is to persuade readers. To accomplish this purpose, writers use persuasive strategies, or appeals. These appeals can be divided into three categories:

header.text: Appeals to ethos, or character, emphasize trustworthiness, credibility, or values shared with the audience. A writer can do this by

elements.text: mentioning personal or professional credentials;
drawing on the established reputation of a person, institution, or brand;
establishing common ground with the audience.

header.text: Appeals to logos, or reason, use logic or verifiable data. A writer can do this by

elements.text: citing relevant and credible statistics, facts, or studies;
explaining the logical chain of reasoning that supports a claim;
anticipating and refuting potential counterclaims.

header.text: Appeals to pathos, or emotion, attempt to activate the audience's emotions. A writer can do this by

elements.text: citing dramatic stories about specific individuals;
appealing to emotions such as fear, guilt, anger, pity, or desire;
choosing words with strong connotations;
using descriptive language to create powerful images.

choices.text: I, for one, refuse to be a trusting sheep led to slaughter or a mindless lemming guided off a cliff.

The experiments of Stanley Milgram have shown that we often defer to authority figures, such as experimenters in lab coats, even when we're dubious about or uncomfortable with what they instruct us to do.

header.text: The first statement is the correct answer. It appeals to pathos, or emotion, by evoking a strong visual image (a trusting sheep led to slaughter and a mindless lemming guided off a cliff).
